extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of Nature (scientists, scholars, and educated public interested in reviews, correspondence, and short research notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards implicit in book reviews, letters, natural-history notes, and an experimental acoustics report — i.e., how to evaluate or produce scientific books, correspondence, species-occurrence notes, etymologies, and acoustical experiments. Emphasises accuracy, up-to-dateness, methodological rigour, and appropriate evidence/citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and modernity of diagrams and apparatus descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams and apparatus descriptions in textbooks should be adequate and of practical service, not 'too brief' or 'far from modern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly brief figure captions and outdated illustrations (examples cited: only Favre and Silbermann calorimeters shown; chromium prepared by Fremy’s method; sulphuric acid concentrated in glass retorts). Provide modern apparatus and clearly useful descriptive detail rather than merely referring to historical experiments (e.g., 'Fig. 5 shows how these tubes were experimented with by Andrews and Tait.' as insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of technical and historical attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical apparatus, processes, and historical attributions must be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not misattribute instruments or processes (criticised examples: 'Bunsen’s eudiometer is ascribed to Cavendish'; 'the Almaden process for the manufacture of mercury is called "Distillation of mercury"'). Check provenance and terminology carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency/up‑to‑datenness of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Works, especially multi-author textbooks, should present modern results and be brought 'completely up-to-date.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect revisions that incorporate recent knowledge and contemporary perspectives (example: the sixth edition of a forensic text was praised for being 'revised throughout' and 'brings it completely up-to-date').

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness of subject‑specific updates (for forensic/taxicology content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialist sections (e.g., insanity, toxicology) should reflect current medical and forensic developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include modern psychiatric views and information on recent/toxic agents of relevance (examples listed: poisoning by salvarsan, tetrachlorethane, T.N.T., gases of warfare) and correct reappraisals of previously held causes (e.g., infections formerly ascribed to ptomaine poisoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual and mathematical accuracy in theoretical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Expositions of physical theories must be conceptually clear and mathematically accurate (for example, when discussing relativity and properties of world-lines/intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misleading statements such as asserting a 'world-line' length is a minimum without proof; define terms like 'straight line', 'inertia lines', 'separation lines' and clarify extremal properties (maximum/minimum/neither) with numerical examples where helpful, as the author cites from earlier work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about foundational assumptions (measurement vs absolute relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should state and justify whether measurement is taken as fundamental or whether more primitive notions (e.g., before/after relations) are used to build measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about foundational choices and show how alternative starting points relate to standard formalisms (the letter references building measurement from absolute 'before and after' relations and contrasts this with common relativist treatments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contemporary natural-history evidence to explain historical or textual accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide plausible, evidence-based natural-history explanations for historical or scriptural narratives when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support explanations with habitat and behavioural data from field studies and authoritative sources (examples: explaining the Gospel 'miraculous draught' by shoaling behaviour of Galilean chromid fishes; citations to Lortet, Tristram, Masterman). Describe plausible sequence of events and behavioural ecology to match the historical account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and traceability in zoological occurrence records
rubrics_metrics.description: Records of species occurrence should give precise habitat description, dates, locality references, and collecting/observation methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide map references (Ordnance Survey sheet and grid), exact positions (e.g., 'near high‑water mark where the Wanson river runs into the sea at the south end of Widemouth Bay'), dates, sample sizes and methods (netting, dredging), species identification, and any distinguishing behaviour; suggest means of further documentation where relevant (e.g., cinematograph to record characteristic movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indicator or guide species and behavioural observations
rubrics_metrics.description: In field searches, employ reliable guide species and record notable behaviours that aid detection and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use presence of the planarian Gunda ulvae as a guide for locating archiannelids, and report behavioural observations (e.g., apparent geotropism demonstrated by rotating stones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic and interpretive accuracy in historical/philological scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations of historical terminology should respect original semantic ranges and not impose modern quantitative meanings where inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: challenge treating 'ilm al‑mizan' ('science of the balance') as quantitative 'Relation und Abwagung des wichtigen Masses' when alchemical usage refers to qualitative adjustment of properties (hotness, dryness). Use original-language sources and specialist literature to justify translations and meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness of manuscript and textual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical claims (e.g., about translations, attributions, forgeries) require careful examination of manuscript evidence and published corpora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite manuscripts (e.g., British Museum Add. 23,418), list important works and translations, compare Arabic texts with Latin counterparts, and avoid broad claims (e.g., that an author is a mere forgery) without studying the corpus comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymological/nominal derivation should be grounded in historical linguistics and original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed derivations of taxonomic names should consult original describers and plausible linguistic roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proposing 'Masaris' derives from Arabic 'Masr' (Egypt) and checking Fabricius (1793) and Agassiz (1845) for whether derivation was indicated; give alternative suggestions only with supporting philological evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory design and calibration for acoustical experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Acoustic testing facilities must have carefully designed, isolated sound chambers and must be calibrated before experimental use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features cited: inner sound chamber insulated from outer shell with separate foundation, rotating steel reflector to equalise sound distribution; calibrate chamber and instruments (e.g., organ) before experiments as 'laborious undertaking' required for reliable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of sound sources appropriate to the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sound sources relevant to the phenomenon under study (e.g., actual noise sources rather than musical tones when studying office noise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: take the click of a typewriter as a source when studying business-office noise rather than relying solely on musical data; consider frequency content and typical real-world signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental apparatus and measurement methods for transmission/reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instruments and arrangements that permit accurate, comparable measures of transmitted and reflected sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include using a parabolic reflector with an organ at the focus, Rayleigh disc resonators to measure transmitted/reflected sound, placing resonators on each side of a partition, and an observer box to avoid disturbance. Ensure test sample areas are of realistic size (tests used panels at least 3 ft. by 5 ft.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for material properties: porosity vs rigidity and their acoustic roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise and report that porosity tends to increase absorption (but may transmit more), whereas rigidity tends to increase reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that absorption efficiency varies with pitch and that small units may perform better; painting porous absorbers tends to reduce their effectiveness by filling pores. Provide comparative data where possible (e.g., reflection: hair felt 6 vs Sackett board 42.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of structural details and small apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Even small openings, ill-fitting doors, or ventilators can drastically reduce sound insulation performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantitative examples (paper cites a 2-inch metal lathe & plaster partition intensity 0.93 vs a 2-inch solid wood door with 3/16-inch clearance 7.3 and with 1/2-inch clearance 11.7); therefore, emphasise fitting and sealing in specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate airborne sound control from structure-borne vibration control
rubrics_metrics.description: Air-wave transmission and solid-borne vibration need different mitigation strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heavy, rigid walling to resist airborne waves; use isolation layers (beds of sand, loose materials) to absorb and prevent transmission of vibrations caused by machinery or footsteps; report floor/ceiling contact transmission separately from air transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reporting and graphical presentation of acoustic results
rubrics_metrics.description: Report measured quantities numerically and illustrate results graphically where informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: give measured times of decay for hearing-aid tests, show graphs of differences with/without instruments, and tabulate relative values of surfaces' absorption for different sounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious generalisation from experimental results
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid over-generalising from specific experimental setups; note limitations and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns 'It would be unwise to generalise too much from the experiments described' and points out variations (e.g., floor behaviour differs from wall behaviour); therefore, specify the domain of applicability of conclusions and call for further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendations for architects and specifiers based on experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate experimental findings into actionable guidance for construction and materials specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of recommendations: aim for absorption to convert sound to heat (linings of felt covered with fabric, light porous tiles, specialised porous plasters), avoid overuse of reflective rigid surfaces for noisy rooms, specify well-fitted doors and attention to small apertures, and be cautious about composite partitions that reduce rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/policy criterion: respect for native customs in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration of native affairs should be conducted with due regard to native customs and institutions and seek sympathetic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical policy points: patient hearing of tribal grievances, remove injustices inflicted under prior regimes, allow opportunity for development in harmony with native culture, and recognise the social role of chiefs and witch-doctors (their authority underpins law and order). Note likely social consequences if traditional beliefs lose their hold.
